content.text: Peugeot Boxer / Citroën Relay P22DTE 2.2 HDi AdBlue & Carbon Failure Representative Case Study Peugeot Boxer 2.2 HDi Motorhome Failure — Why Repeated Limp Mode Events Led to an Engine Replacement A premium visual breakdown of how an AdBlue warning, ignored limp modes, and carbon contamination led to a £3,600 reconditioned engine. “We were halfway through the NC500 in Scotland. The motorhome was fully loaded — camping gear, kids, dog. Then the ‘AdBlue system fault’ message appeared, followed by ‘Engine fault: repair needed.’ Then the countdown started: 700 miles before the engine would refuse to start. We limped to a garage in Inverness. The mechanic said, ‘The EGR is clogged solid with carbon. The engine is in bad shape. A replacement is going to be cheaper than trying to fix this one.’” Compare Boxer Repair Quotes See the Failure Timeline 85k Failure mileage AdBlue System fault Carbon Contamination £3,600 Recon engine 12 mo Warranty Case summary A 2017 Peugeot Boxer motorhome with 85,000 miles and an AdBlue system failure that led to carbon contamination. The owner ignored repeated limp mode events and countdown warnings. By the time the motorhome reached a specialist, the EGR was clogged, the NOx sensor had failed, and carbon had contaminated the entire engine. Model Peugeot Boxer (2017) / Citroën Relay Engine P22DTE 2.2 HDi (DW12 family) Mileage at failure 85,000 miles Service history Main dealer annually, but used primarily for summer touring Primary use Motorhome — long periods of sitting idle (6–8 months per year) Disclaimer: This is an illustrative representative scenario based on workshop consensus and known PSA diesel failure patterns [INDUSTRY ESTIMATE]. Individual outcomes vary. Early warning The whole disaster started with an AdBlue warning light. The owner topped up AdBlue, but the warning didn't clear. Repeated limp mode events followed. Each reset bought time, but carbon contamination worsened until the engine needed replacement. What owner thought “Just top up AdBlue” The motorhome still drove, so the symptom did not feel urgent. What it actually was EGR clogged + NOx sensor failed Carbon build-up prevented proper regens, leading to extensive internal contamination. Why it matters Engine replacement Once carbon has contaminated pistons, rings, and turbo, repair often costs more than replacement. If your motorhome diesel develops an AdBlue warning that does not clear within 50 miles of refilling, have the NOx sensors and AdBlue system diagnosed immediately. Ignoring repeated limp mode events can lead to extensive carbon contamination and engine replacement. Failure timeline From AdBlue warning to engine replacement in just 3,000 miles. This case is a classic motorhome emissions-system failure: the owner ignored the warning signs and paid the price. What the owner noticed AdBlue warning at 82k, repeated limp mode events, countdown timer, and permanent power loss at 85k. What was happening internally EGR clogged, NOx sensor failed, carbon built up on pistons and rings, causing low compression and turbo contamination. “The mechanic said, ‘Look, I can strip your engine down and see if it’s salvageable. That’s £700 in labour before I’ve even ordered a single part. Or I can fit a reconditioned engine for £3,600 all-in with a warranty. Which sounds smarter to you-’ He was right. The reconditioned engine has been perfect for 10,000 miles.” 82,000 miles AdBlue warning appears 85,000 miles Permanent limp mode on NC500 Specialist Reconditioned engine fitted Workshop diagnosis The EGR was clogged, the NOx sensor had failed, and carbon had contaminated the engine. The specialist read fault codes, performed a compression test, and borescoped the engine. The findings revealed extensive carbon contamination and low compression on two cylinders. NOx sensor Failed — generating incorrect readings EGR valve Clogged with carbon deposits — stuck partially open AdBlue system Multiple logged faults Compression test Low on two cylinders Borescope Heavy carbon build-up on piston crowns and cylinder walls Turbocharger Signs of carbon debris contamination Oil condition Thick, black, contaminated Specialist summary “The motorhome has sat idle for long periods between trips. The EGR system has clogged with carbon. The NOx sensor failed, which meant the engine management couldn’t properly manage regeneration cycles. The repeated limp mode events were a symptom, but now we’re looking at extensive carbon contamination, low compression, and a turbo that may fail soon. The cost of repairing this engine properly exceeds the cost of fitting a reconditioned exchange unit. A replacement is the more economical option.” Repair options Scrap the motorhome, used engine, repair existing, reconditioned engine, or dealer new. Compare the routes the owner faced after diagnosis. The reconditioned engine is selected by default because that was the chosen route. Hidden carbon damage could be extensive. With low compression and carbon build-up, the specialist could not know whether the piston rings had seized or the bores had been scored without a full strip-down. Path A Full strip-down and inspection of existing engine — 10 hours labour (£650–£800). Then repair or replace based on findings. £650–£800 Additional repair costs if bottom end damage found. Path B Fit reconditioned exchange engine. No inspection uncertainty. Faster turnaround. £2,500–£4,000 Known cost, known warranty, faster turnaround. The owner chose Path B. The reconditioned engine cost less than the upper estimate of repairing the existing unit, came with a warranty, and had the motorhome back on the road in 6 days rather than 2–3 weeks. Fork in the road The owner had to decide: strip and inspect, or fit a reconditioned engine. The motorhome was worth approximately £25,000–£35,000 before failure. A £3,600 reconditioned engine represented 10–14% of its value — a justifiable repair for a leisure vehicle. Scrap the motorhome Path 1 Sell as spares/repair — return £1,000–£3,000. Repair cost estimate £3,500–£5,000+ Reconditioned unit was cheaper or equal to the lower estimate, without the risk of hidden damage. Turnaround time 6 days vs 10-15+ Owner wanted the motorhome back quickly for summer touring. £3,600 Total paid Reconditioned engine fitted by independent specialist. A reconditioned engine provided a known cost, warranty, and faster return to the road. Outcome What happened after the reconditioned engine was fitted- Six days later, the motorhome was back on the road. The owner now services annually regardless of mileage and uses the motorhome monthly for short runs. Final cost £3,600 Main dealer new engine quote £6,000–£9,000+ Savings £2,400–£5,400+ Lead time 6 days New maintenance schedule Annual service regardless of mileage; monthly short runs Long-term result 10,000 miles trouble-free “For motorhomes, an exchange engine is often the fastest and most cost-effective resolution. The specialist had a reconditioned unit on my pallet within three days. Trying to rebuild an engine clogged with carbon would have taken weeks and cost more.” Lessons learned If your motorhome diesel develops an AdBlue warning, don't ignore it. Address it immediately. The commercial lesson is simple: emissions-system failures are cheaper when caught early. Ignoring repeated limp mode events allows carbon build-up to continue, leading to extensive internal contamination. Annual service regardless of mileage £200–£500 Prevents carbon build-up from long idle periods. Strip and clean existing engine £3,500–£5,000+ Labour-intensive, risk of hidden damage, longer downtime. Reconditioned exchange engine £2,500–£4,000 Known-good unit, warranty, faster turnaround. Main dealer new engine £6,000–£9,000+ Avoid at all costs — independent options exist. A £3,600 reconditioned engine on a £30,000 motorhome is 12% of its value — a justifiable repair. A £7,500 main dealer new engine is 25% — harder to justify.
